caption: The essay funnels a wide worry about conscious AI into three psychological biases that converge on 'it's pareidolia,' then into four independent arguments that converge on 'functionalism is shaky,' then forks into two distinct ethical risks, before looping back to its opening warning that mistaking machines for us means underestimating ourselves.
title: Converge, Fork, Return

scenes.title: Overview: temptation, argument, ethics, loop
scenes.caption: Two converging clusters (why we're tempted; why we should doubt it) lead into a fork of distinct risks, which closes by returning to the opening stakes.

items.detail: Consciousness brings moral status; getting this wrong distorts ethics either way.

items.label: WHY WE'RE TEMPTED TO SEE IT

items.detail: Three overlapping biases make us see human qualities as definitional.
LLMs pull our strings via language; AlphaFold doesn't, though it's similar under the hood.

items.sub: every point feels like a threshold
items.detail: Exponential curves and dreams of digital immortality inflate expectations.

items.text: Mostly pareidolia — but that's only step one
items.detail: Recognizing the bias doesn't settle whether real artificial consciousness is possible.
The whole case for conscious AI rests on this usually-unexamined assumption.
No clean separation of mindware and wetware exists in real brains.
Continuous, analogue, and dynamical processes may matter more than algorithms.
Consciousness may be tied to self-sustaining, living, predictive bodies.
A simulated storm doesn't get anything wet; mind-uploading assumes its conclusion.
Each argument stands alone but together they weaken the case for conscious AI.

items.text: Given the uncertainty, don't build it
items.detail: Deliberately creating conscious AI would risk new, uncontrollable suffering.

items.text: If AI really is conscious: disaster
items.sub: new suffering, hard to switch off
items.detail: Rights would make dangerous systems harder to control or shut down.

items.text: If it only seems conscious: illusion persists
items.detail: Like a visual illusion, the feeling of AI consciousness survives knowing better.

items.text: Recover a soul that's more breath than machine
items.detail: Mistaking algorithms for minds means overestimating them and underestimating ourselves.

scenes.title: Inside: why we're tempted
scenes.caption: One conflation (intelligence with consciousness) branches into three biases, each with its own mechanism, all converging on the same conclusion: this is pareidolia.

items.text: Intelligence is doing; consciousness is being
items.detail: Nagel: 'something it is like to be' an organism — a different property from problem-solving.
Taking the human example as definitional rather than one case among many.
Placing humans atop every hierarchy, then projecting human traits onto machines.
LLMs, not protein-folders like AlphaFold, get called conscious — because they talk.
Better word: 'confabulate' — doing, not experiencing.
On an exponential curve, every point feels like an inflection point.
Ex Machina: 'that's the history of Gods' — the lure of building minds forever.
Magical AI narratives help justify valuations and salaries too.

items.text: Recognizing pareidolia is only step one
items.detail: Seeing why we're fooled doesn't yet tell us whether artificial consciousness is possible.

scenes.title: Inside: four arguments against functionalism
scenes.caption: One assumption feeds four independent two-step arguments — Turing brains, alternative dynamics, life, and simulation — that converge on the same shaky conclusion.

items.detail: Computational functionalism, so ingrained it's rarely recognized as an assumption.
A universal Turing machine can run any algorithm on any suitable substrate.

items.text: But brains have no such split
items.detail: What a brain does and what it is cannot be cleanly separated.
Electromagnetic fields, neurotransmitter flux — none strictly Turing-computable.
A 'computational' version of the governor would misunderstand what's going on.
Conscious experience as the brain's best guess, calibrated by sensory signals.
Prediction-error minimization is inseparable from the materiality of metabolism.

items.text: A simulated storm doesn't get you wet
items.detail: Simulation lacks the causal powers of the thing simulated.
You're no more likely to exist in the sim than a hailstorm is to arise in a weather computer.
Four independent lines each weaken computational functionalism, and together they compound.
